rows.selection_reason: With no prior experiments completed, there is zero evidence about which design choices matter. The most informative first experiment is a clean, minimal baseline that anchors the configuration space. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest RNA-only configuration using the most standard encoder (PCA) and the simplest profile setting. It establishes a reference performance level for the RNA modality, confirms the pipeline runs correctly, and provides a baseline against which all other modalities (image-only, multimodal) and more complex encoders (scvi, scgpt) can be compared. Under a limited budget, starting with the lowest-risk, most interpretable baseline reduces the risk of a failed first run and gives a clear anchor for subsequent exploration of image modality, multimodal fusion, and advanced encoders.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000 at ~48.5% accuracy), the dominant uncertainty is which modality carries the most discriminative signal. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly compares the image modality against the RNA baseline while holding profile_setting constant, isolating the modality effect. If image_only substantially outperforms rna_only, the search should pivot toward image-centric and multimodal configurations; if it performs comparably or worse, RNA-based improvements (better encoders, multiprofile) become the priority. This is the highest-impact, highest-uncertainty design decision in the space, and resolving it first maximizes the information gained per experiment under a tight budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image-only, singleprofile, resnet50) is much weaker at 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. The key uncertainty is whether moving from singleprofile to multiprofile (with aggregation) meaningfully improves RNA representation. config_002 tests exactly this: it is the minimal change from config_001 (singleprofile → multiprofile + avgpool), isolating the effect of multi-profile aggregation. This is the best next experiment because (1) it directly ablates a design axis that pervades the entire configuration space—knowing whether multiprofile helps determines whether to invest future budget in multiprofile multimodal configs or stick with singleprofile, (2) avgpool is the simplest aggregation, giving a clean signal before trying transformer, and (3) it reduces uncertainty about a high-leverage decision before committing to more complex multimodal experiments.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved the best result so far (acc=0.591, F1=0.573), a substantial +10.6% improvement over singleprofile (config_001, acc=0.485). This confirms multiprofile aggregation is a critical design lever. Uncertainty: We have only tested avgpool as the aggregation method; it is unknown whether a transformer-based aggregation would further improve performance or whether simple averaging is already near-optimal. This experiment (config_003) isolates the aggregation variable by changing only avgpool→transformer while holding everything else at the known-best setting (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000). Why this is the best next step: (1) It is a controlled one-variable extension of the current best result, maximizing information per experiment. (2) The aggregation method is a fundamental architectural choice that will propagate to all future multiprofile and multimodal experiments—knowing whether transformer adds value narrows the search space substantially. (3) If transformer significantly outperforms avgpool, it signals that learned aggregation is worth the extra complexity and should be prioritized in multimodal configs; if they are comparable, avgpool suffices and we can focus budget on RNA encoder choice and multimodal fusion. This reduces uncertainty about a high-impact design decision before committing experiments to the larger multimodal grid.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with pca_n2000 and avgpool (config_002) is the clear best at 0.591 acc, while image-only resnet50 (config_010) is very weak at 0.208 acc. This raises the critical question of whether the image modality contains any complementary signal that can improve beyond the strong RNA baseline. Config_018 directly extends our best configuration by adding resnet50 image features via simple concatenation, the most standard and interpretable fusion. It is the most informative next step because: (1) it tests the single most important open question—whether multimodal fusion adds value over the best unimodal result; (2) concat is the simplest fusion, so if it fails to beat 0.591, we gain strong evidence that the image signal is too weak/noisy to be useful regardless of fusion strategy; (3) it uses the already-characterized resnet50 encoder, isolating the fusion question from encoder choice. Under a limited budget, this single experiment most efficiently reduces uncertainty about the core design decision of whether to pursue multimodal fusion at all.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multi-profile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc, only marginally above RNA-only avgpool (0.591). The image-only model was very weak (0.208), raising uncertainty about whether the image features are contributing at all or being diluted. The fusion mechanism is the one design axis not yet varied in the multimodal setting. Question: Does weighted fusion (config_019) outperform concat, indicating that modality-level scaling/balancing is important given the large gap in per-modality signal strength? Why best next step: It is a single-variable ablation of the current best config, directly testing whether the simple concatenation is optimal or whether explicit weighting can better leverage the (apparently weaker) image branch. This is low-risk, high-information: a positive result opens the weighted-fusion family across encoders/profiles, while a null result confirms concat suffices and redirects budget toward stronger image encoders or RNA encoders.

Evidence: The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses PCA n2000 as the RNA encoder within a multimodal multi-profile avgpool weighted-fusion setup. RNA is the dominant signal (RNA-only 0.591 vs image-only 0.208), yet we have only tested one RNA encoder (PCA, a simple linear projection). This leaves major uncertainty about whether a learned nonlinear embedding could substantially improve the RNA branch. Question: Does scvi_n200 (a learned nonlinear latent embedding) outperform PCA n2000 in the best multimodal configuration? Config_031 changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_019, making it a clean single-variable comparison. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly probes the highest-impact untested design axis (RNA encoder quality) within the already-validated best architecture, so a positive result immediately yields a new best configuration, while a negative result rules out scvi and focuses remaining budget on scgpt or the image encoder. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The RNA encoder choice has shown the largest single-factor improvement so far (pca_n2000 → scvi_n200 yielded +3.9% acc in the multimodal setting: 0.639 → 0.678). The current best config (config_031: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted, resnet50) achieves 0.678 acc. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether scgpt, a more expressive pre-trained RNA encoder, can further improve on scvi_n200 in this multimodal context. Question tested: Does replacing scvi_n200 with scgpt (all other hyperparameters held at their known-best values: multiprofile, avgpool, weighted, resnet50) yield a further accuracy gain? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable extension of the most productive design axis identified so far (RNA encoder quality), keeps all other knobs at their validated optima, and directly determines whether the RNA encoder dimension still has headroom to exploit before investing budget in less-certain axes like the image encoder (which showed very weak standalone signal at 0.208 acc).

Evidence: config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the current best at 0.678 acc, clearly outperforming pca_n2000 (0.639) and scgpt (0.525) under identical settings. Multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion are well-supported. The only major untested dimension in this best-configuration context is the image encoder: only resnet50 has been used, while imagenet_vit_l remains unexplored. Image-only resnet50 was very weak (0.208), but in multimodal fusion it contributed meaningfully (0.591→0.639 with pca; 0.639→0.678 with scvi), suggesting the image branch carries complementary signal. Testing config_037 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) directly asks whether a stronger, higher-capacity image encoder can further boost the multimodal pipeline beyond the current best. This is the highest-value next experiment because it exploits the strongest known configuration while probing the single largest unexplored design axis, and the result will inform whether further investment in image-side capacity is warranted.

Evidence: The current best is config_037 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) at 0.706 acc. All multimodal experiments so far have used avgpool aggregation; transformer aggregation has only been tested in RNA-only settings where it underperformed avgpool by ~7 points (0.519 vs 0.591). However, in the multimodal context with a strong ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation might capture cross-profile interactions that avgpool averages away, potentially complementing the image signal differently. Question: Does transformer aggregation improve upon avgpool in the multimodal+ViT-L+scvi_n200+weighted setting? Why this experiment: It is the single most informative next step because (1) it is a minimal, controlled change from the current best (only aggregation differs), isolating the effect of one design variable; (2) if it improves, it identifies a new promising direction; if it does not, it definitively rules out transformer aggregation for the top-performing family, saving future budget from exploring dead ends; (3) under a limited budget, confirming or refuting the best aggregation strategy at the highest-performing operating point maximizes information per experiment.
